1.note: Here, **many days** represents a long period of time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And it was a long time] or [And a long time passed]
See how you translated the similar expression in 6:11. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh spoke a message to Elijah]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **in the third year**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [after three years]
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:14. Alternate translation: [on the surface of the earth]

2.note: The author is providing background information about the severity of the famine to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

3.q: עֹבַדְיָ֖הוּ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל־הַ⁠בָּ֑יִת וְ⁠עֹבַדְיָ֗הוּ הָיָ֥ה יָרֵ֛א אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה מְאֹֽד
3.note: in this verse and the next verse, the author is introducing **Obadiah** as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation.
See how you translated the similar expression in 16:9. Alternate translation: [who was in charge of the palace] or [the administrator of his palace]

4.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 11:6. Alternate translation: [when Jezebel killed the prophets of Yahweh]

The author is using **50 men in the cave** as a common expression of his culture to mean that Obadiah hid 50 men in each of two caves. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by fifties in each of two caves]

The author is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, and in verse 13. Alternate translation: [with food]

5.note: In this verse, the terms **horse** and **mule** are singular in form, but they refer to several horses and mules that might be kept alive. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation. Alternate translation: [some of the horses and mules]

Ahab is speaking as if they might actually **cut off** the cattle, as if they were part of a plant or tree. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and we will not have to kill any of the cattle]

6.q: אַחְאָ֞ב הָלַ֨ךְ בְּ⁠דֶ֤רֶךְ אֶחָד֙ לְ⁠בַדּ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠עֹֽבַדְיָ֛הוּ הָלַ֥ךְ בְּ⁠דֶרֶךְ־אֶחָ֖ד לְ⁠בַדּֽ⁠וֹ
6.note: It might seem that repeating the expression **by himself** would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, you could represent this expression only once. Alternate translation: [Each of them went in a separate way by himself]

7.note: See the discussion in the Introduction to 1 Kings of this sense of the word **behold**. Alternate translation: [and suddenly Elijah]

In each instance, the pronoun **he** refers to Obadiah. The pronoun **him** refers to Elijah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Obadiah recognized Elijah, and Obadiah fell on his face]

Be sure that it is clear in your translation that Obadiah did not fall down accidentally. He knelt down in front of Elijah, pressing his face to the ground, as a gesture to honor him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action. Alternate translation: [and he knelt down and pressed his face to the ground in front of Elijah in order to show him great honor]

8.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Go and tell your master that I have returned]

If Obadiah said exactly this, he would leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Elijah has returned]

9.q: מֶ֣ה חָטָ֑אתִי כִּֽי־אַתָּ֞ה נֹתֵ֧ן אֶֽת־עַבְדְּ⁠ךָ֛ בְּ⁠יַד־אַחְאָ֖ב לַ⁠הֲמִיתֵֽ⁠נִי
9.note: Obadiah is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I have not sinned, that you should put your servant into the hand of Ahab to kill me!]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that you are giving Ahab the occasion to use his power to kill me, your servant]

Obadiah is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, your servant,]

10.q: חַ֣י ׀ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֗י⁠ךָ אִם־יֶשׁ־גּ֤וֹי וּ⁠מַמְלָכָה֙ אֲ֠שֶׁר לֹֽא־שָׁלַ֨ח אֲדֹנִ֥⁠י שָׁם֙ לְ⁠בַקֶּשְׁ⁠ךָ֔
10.note: Following the custom of his culture, Obadiah is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. In a context such as this, it may be natural to express just the first part of the condition as a negative statement. See how you translated the similar expression “if he will kill his servant” in 1:51. Alternate translation: [I swear by Yahweh your God that there is not a nation or kingdom where my master has not sent to seek you there]

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [where my master has not sent to seek you]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [If they said that you were not there]

Obadiah, in summarizing the replies of leaders to Ahab, is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He is not here]

Here, **the kingdom or the nation** represents the ruler of a kingdom or nation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the leader of the kingdom or the nation]

11.q: וְ⁠עַתָּ֖ה אַתָּ֣ה אֹמֵ֑ר לֵ֛ךְ אֱמֹ֥ר לַ⁠אדֹנֶ֖י⁠ךָ הִנֵּ֥ה אֵלִיָּֽהוּ
11.note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what Obadiah said, continuing from the previous two verses (level 1). Obadiah is quoting what Elijah said (level 2). This includes something that Elijah wanted Obadiah to tell Ahab (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there is not a second-level or third-level quotation.

11.q: וְ⁠עַתָּ֖ה אַתָּ֣ה אֹמֵ֑ר לֵ֛ךְ אֱמֹ֥ר לַ⁠אדֹנֶ֖י⁠ךָ הִנֵּ֥ה אֵלִיָּֽהוּ
11.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there are not quotations within quotations. Alternate translation: [And now you are telling me to go and say to my master that you are here]

12.note: Obadiah is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will go** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what he will do and what he expects the **Spirit of Yahweh** will do. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [For my part, I will go from with you]

13.q: הֲ⁠לֹֽא־הֻגַּ֤ד לַֽ⁠אדֹנִ⁠י֙ אֵ֣ת אֲשֶׁר־עָשִׂ֔יתִי בַּ⁠הֲרֹ֣ג אִיזֶ֔בֶל אֵ֖ת נְבִיאֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וָ⁠אַחְבִּא֩ מִ⁠נְּבִיאֵ֨י יְהוָ֜ה מֵ֣אָה אִ֗ישׁ חֲמִשִּׁ֨ים חֲמִשִּׁ֥ים אִישׁ֙ בַּ⁠מְּעָרָ֔ה וָ⁠אֲכַלְכְּלֵ֖⁠ם לֶ֥חֶם וָ⁠מָֽיִם
13.note: Obadiah is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Certainly it has been declared to my master what I did when Jezebel killed the prophets of Yahweh, that I hid 100 men from the prophets of Yahweh, 50, 50 men in the cave, and I sustained them with bread and water!]

Even though Obadiah is addressing Elijah directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **my lord** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [to you, my lord,]
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:4. Alternate translation: [by fifties in each of two caves]

14.q: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ אַתָּ֣ה אֹמֵ֔ר לֵ֛ךְ אֱמֹ֥ר לַֽ⁠אדֹנֶ֖י⁠ךָ הִנֵּ֣ה אֵלִיָּ֑הוּ וַ⁠הֲרָגָֽ⁠נִי
14.note: See how you punctuated the similar sentence in 8:11.

14.q: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ אַתָּ֣ה אֹמֵ֔ר לֵ֛ךְ אֱמֹ֥ר לַֽ⁠אדֹנֶ֖י⁠ךָ הִנֵּ֣ה אֵלִיָּ֑הוּ
14.note: You may have chosen to translate the similar sentence in 8:11 so that there would not be quotations within quotations. If so, you can do the same thing here. Alternate translation: [And now you are telling me to go and say to my master that you are here]

15.note: Following the custom of his culture, Elijah is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred. **The life of Yahweh of Armies** is a way of swearing by Yahweh himself, indicating that Elijah is making a solemn promise that he considers binding and sacred. Alternate translation: [I swear by Yahweh of Armies]
See how you translated the similar expression in [17:1](ta:17). Alternate translation: [whose servant I am]

18.note: Elijah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but rather you and the house of your father have troubled Israel]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:31. Alternate translation: [your extended family]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:5. Alternate translation: [and worshiping]

Elijah is probably using the plural term **Baals** because the Israelites were worshiping multiple manifestations or representations of Baal. Various places had their own shrines or temples in which they worshiped local representations, such as Baal of Tyre, Baal of Peor, etc. Since the name is singular in the rest of the book, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could use the singular here as well. Alternate translation: [Baal]

19.note: **And now** was an expression that speakers in this culture commonly used to introduce their main topic. See how you have been translating it in contexts such as 1:12 and 2:16.

Elijah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [send messengers and gather]

Elijah is saying **all Israel** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [representatives from throughout Israel]

Here, **eaters at the table of Jezebel** represents prophets whom Jezebel supported. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [whom Jezebel supports] or [for whom Jezebel provides from the royal treasury]

20.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And Ahab sent messengers among all of the sons of Israel to summon their leaders]
See how you translated the similar expression in [6:1](ta:06). Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

21.note: Elijah is using the question form to challenge and rebuke the people of Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have been limping on two opinions for long enough!] or [You should not be limping on two opinions any longer!]

Elijah is speaking as if the people were actually **limping** on these **opinions**, shifting their weight back and forth between them as a limping person does with his legs. He means that they are being indecisive about whether to worship Yahweh or Baal. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will you be wavering back and forth between two faiths]
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:18. Alternate translation: [worship him … worship him]

Here, **a word** represents something the people might have said by using words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [But the people did not say anything in response to him]

22.note: Elijah is stating the pronoun **I** separately in order to emphasize a contrast between himself and the prophets of Baal. To translate this expression and the similar ones in the next two verses, see how you translated the expression “I, I will go” in 18:12, which similarly emphasizes a contrast. Alternate translation: [For my part, I remain a prophet of Yahweh]

23.note: Elijah is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Now let two bulls be given to us]
The pronoun **them** refers to the prophets of Baal. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and let the prophets of Baal choose]

24.q: וּ⁠קְרָאתֶ֞ם בְּ⁠שֵׁ֣ם אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠כֶ֗ם וַֽ⁠אֲנִי֙ אֶקְרָ֣א בְ⁠שֵׁם־יְהוָ֔ה
24.note: Elijah is using **call on the name of** as a common expression of his culture to mean “pray to by name.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And you will call upon your god by name, and for my part, I will call upon Yahweh by name] or [And you will pray to your god by name, and for my part, I will pray to Yahweh by name here and in the next verse]

Elijah had been speaking to the gathered Israelite leaders, but here he turns to address the prophets of Baal, so the pronoun **you** refers to them. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And you prophets of Baal will call]
Here, **word** represents what Elijah said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What you have said is good]

25.q: בַּחֲר֨וּ לָ⁠כֶ֜ם הַ⁠פָּ֤ר הָֽ⁠אֶחָד֙ וַ⁠עֲשׂ֣וּ רִאשֹׁנָ֔ה כִּ֥י אַתֶּ֖ם הָ⁠רַבִּ֑ים
25.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since you are many, choose for yourselves one bull, and prepare it first]

26.note: The author that readers will know that he means someone **gave** this **bull** to the prophets of Baal when they chose it. An important aspect of this contest was allowing those prophets every advantage. No one chose a bull for them and **gave** it to them. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [that one gave to them when they chose it]

The author is using the pronoun **one** in a general sense, not to refer to a specific person. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that was given to them]

26.q: וְ⁠אֵ֥ין ק֖וֹל וְ⁠אֵ֣ין עֹנֶ֑ה וַֽ⁠יְפַסְּח֔וּ עַל־הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֖חַ אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָֽׂה
26.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that **they limped beside the altar** before the information that there was **no voice, and no answering**, since these prophets were limping around the altar as they **called** to Baal. Alternate translation: [And they limped beside the altar that one had made. But there was no voice, and there was no answering]

Here, **voice** represents someone speaking or responding. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [But no one said anything or did anything in response]

In this context, the word **limped** probably describes an ecstatic, rhythmic, and jerky or hopping dance that was part of the worship ritual of the prophets of Baal. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And they danced jerkily]

Some ancient manuscripts read “one had made.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “they had made.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

27.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since he is a god, call out with a great voice]

Elijah actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying. He does not believe that Baal is really a god, and he is mocking the prophets for thinking that he is. If a speaker of your language would not say the opposite of what he meant for such a purpose, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [since you think that he is a god]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **contemplation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he is contemplating something]

Elijah is using this phrase as a polite way of referring to an activity that is done in private. Your language may have a similar expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [he is going to the bathroom]
Here, **a way** represents “a journey.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he is on a journey]

29.note: In this context, the word **prophesied** does not indicate that these prophets of Baal said things that Baal inspired them to say. Instead, the word describes people being in a raving state in which they are not in full control of their actions. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the same term in 1 Samuel 18:10, where it describes Saul attempting to use violence against David while out of control. Alternate translation: [that they raved]

Here, **the offering of the grain offering** represents the time when the grain offering was customarily made. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [until the time when it was customary to offer the grain offering]

The author assumes that readers will know that the time when the daily grain offering was made was in the middle of the afternoon. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [until the middle of the afternoon]
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:26. Alternate translation: [But no one said anything or did anything or paid any attention in response]

30.note: The term **broken-down** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the altar of Yahweh that people had broken down]

31.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 6:11. Alternate translation: [to whom Yahweh had spoken a message]

32.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:2. Alternate translation: [for the worship of Yahweh]

The author is using **like the house of two seahs of seed** as a common expression of his culture to mean that this trench was big enough to hold two seahs of seed. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [big enough to hold two seahs of seed]

Each of these **seahs** was equivalent to nearly eight liters or about a quarter of a bushel. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “seah” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

34.note: The implication is that the people obeyed Elijah’s command and poured the water on the sacrifice and on the wood. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and on the wood.” And they did]

The author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And someone did that a second time] or [and that was done again]

36.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 18:29. Alternate translation: [at the time when it was customary to offer the grain offering]

The expression **let it be known** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [make known]
Here, **word** represents what God had commanded by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and at your command]

37.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please answer me]

Elijah is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have turned** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the personal role of Yahweh in turning the **heart** of the **people** back to himself. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. See how you translated the similar expression “you, you swore” in 1:17. Alternate translation: [you are the one who has turned their heart back]

Elijah is using the past tense to describe something that is ongoing in the present. He is doing that in order to show that it will certainly be accomplished. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a different tense. Alternate translation: [you are the one who is turning their heart back]

Elijah is speaking as if Yahweh had actually **turned the heart** of the people in a different direction, as if the heart were an object that could be physically rotated. He means that God has caused the people to trust in him again. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you have caused them to trust in you again] or [and you are the one who is causing them to trust in you again]

In this verse, the word **heart** is singular in form, but it refers to the hearts of all the people. If it would be helpful in your language, if you decide to retain this image, you could use the plural form of “heart.” Alternate translation: [their hearts]

38.note: The author is speaking as if the fire actually **licked up** the water. The image suggests that the fire consumed the water completely, just as an animal might lick up liquid. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it evaporated]

39.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 18:7. Alternate translation: [and they knelt down and pressed their faces to the ground in order to show Yahweh great honor]

39.q: יְהוָה֙ ה֣וּא הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֔ים יְהוָ֖ה ה֥וּא הָ⁠אֱלֹהִֽים
39.note: The author is repeating the phrase **Yahweh, he is God!** to depict people throughout the crowd of Israelites coming to this realization and shouting it out. The people are not chanting the quoted phrase all at the same time, but rather one after another in the crowd is shouting it. If the repetition would instead suggest to your readers that the people were chanting this repeatedly, you could express the meaning in another way. The UST models one way to do that.

40.note: The author is using one person who was involved in this action, Elijah, calling him **he**, to represent everyone who was involved. The people seized and killed the prophets, but Elijah, as the one who ordered this, is credited with the action. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he had the people slaughter them there]

41.q: עֲלֵ֖ה אֱכֹ֣ל וּ⁠שְׁתֵ֑ה כִּי־ק֖וֹל הֲמ֥וֹן הַ⁠גָּֽשֶׁם
41.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since there is the sound of the roar of a shower, go up, eat and drink]

42.note: The author is using the term **head** to mean the “top” of Mount **Carmel**. If this term does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the top of Mount Carmel]

42.q: וַ⁠יִּגְהַ֣ר אַ֔רְצָ⁠ה וַ⁠יָּ֥שֶׂם פָּנָ֖י⁠ו בֵּ֥ין ברכ⁠ו
42.note: Elijah **bowed down to the ground** and **put his face between his knees** as a symbolic action by which he showed humility and earnestness in prayer before Yahweh while waiting for rain. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he bowed down low in earnest prayer, not even looking around]

43.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Elijah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Elijah said, “Return,”]

44.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **the seventh time**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [on time seven] or [on the last time]

The implication is that the cloud was appearing at the distant horizon where the sea met the sky, so it appeared to be **coming up from the sea**. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [is now visible just above the horizon]

44.q: עֲלֵ֨ה אֱמֹ֤ר אֶל־אַחְאָב֙ אֱסֹ֣ר וָ⁠רֵ֔ד וְ⁠לֹ֥א יַעַצָרְ⁠כָ֖ה הַ⁠גָּֽשֶׁם
44.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Go up and tell Ahab to harness and go down so the rain does not stop him]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [So the rain does not stop you, harness and go down]

Elijah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Harness your horses to your chariot]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a respectful recommendation rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a respectful recommendation. Alternate translation: [You should harness your horses to your chariot] or [You should have your servants harness your horses to your chariot]

45.note: The author is using **to thus and to thus** as a common expression of his culture to mean that what he describes happened very quickly. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [very quickly]

The phrase **clouds and wind** expresses a single idea. The word **wind** tells more about these **clouds**, specifically, that the wind drove them in from the sea. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [with wind-driven clouds]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And Ahab rode in his chariot]

46.note: Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the power of Yahweh]

The author is speaking as if the hand of Yahweh was actually **on** Elijah. He means that Yahweh gave Elijah supernatural strength and power. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [empowered Elijah]
Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of Ahab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [ahead of Ahab]

The author is using **your coming to Jezreel** as a common expression of his culture to mean “the entrance of Jezreel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the entrance of Jezreel]
